cards.english: How does the browser render a page (critical rendering path)?
cards.word: Parse HTML→DOM, CSS→CSSOM, combine into render tree, layout, then paint
cards.grammarNote: The **DOM** and **CSSOM** merge into a render tree; the browser computes geometry (**layout/reflow**), then **paints** pixels, and **composites** layers. CSS is render-blocking and synchronous `<script>` blocks parsing, so their placement and size directly affect first paint.

cards.english: What's the difference between reflow and repaint?
cards.word: Reflow recomputes layout/geometry; repaint just redraws pixels
cards.grammarNote: **Reflow (layout)** happens when geometry changes (size, position, adding nodes) and is expensive because it can cascade. **Repaint** happens for visual-only changes (color) — cheaper. Animating `transform`/`opacity` avoids both by staying on the **compositor**, which is why they're the performant properties to animate.

cards.english: How does the JavaScript event loop work?
cards.word: A single thread runs the call stack, then drains microtasks, then one macrotask, and repeats
cards.grammarNote: JS is single-threaded. Synchronous code runs on the **call stack**; async callbacks queue as **macrotasks** (timers, I/O) or **microtasks** (promises). After the stack empties, the loop drains **all microtasks**, then takes one macrotask, then renders. This is why a promise resolves before a `setTimeout(0)`.

cards.english: Explain event bubbling and delegation.
cards.word: Events propagate up the DOM; delegation puts one listener on a parent
cards.grammarNote: After firing on the target, events **bubble** up ancestors (there's also a capture phase down). **Event delegation** exploits this: attach a single listener to a container and inspect `event.target`, instead of binding many child listeners — efficient for dynamic lists. `stopPropagation()` halts bubbling.

cards.english: Compare cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage.
cards.word: Cookies go to the server each request; localStorage/sessionStorage are client-only
cards.grammarNote: **Cookies** (~4KB) are sent with every request — right for session tokens (use `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`). **localStorage** persists across sessions, JS-accessible, ~5–10MB, never auto-sent. **sessionStorage** is the same but cleared when the tab closes. Don't store secrets in web storage (XSS-readable).

cards.english: Compare CSR, SSR, SSG, and ISR.
cards.word: Client-render, server-render per request, pre-build at deploy, or rebuild on a schedule
cards.grammarNote: **CSR** ships JS that renders in the browser (fast navigations, slow first paint, weaker SEO). **SSR** renders HTML per request (good SEO/TTFB, server cost). **SSG** pre-renders at build (fastest, static). **ISR** regenerates static pages in the background on an interval — SSG freshness without full rebuilds.

cards.english: What's the difference between debounce and throttle?
cards.word: Debounce waits for a pause; throttle caps to once per interval
cards.grammarNote: **Debounce** delays execution until events stop for N ms — ideal for search-as-you-type or resize-end. **Throttle** runs at most once per interval regardless of event frequency — ideal for scroll or mousemove handlers. Both limit how often expensive handlers fire.

cards.english: What are the basics of web accessibility (a11y)?
cards.word: Semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, alt text, ARIA, and sufficient contrast
cards.grammarNote: Use **semantic elements** (`<button>`, `<nav>`) so assistive tech understands structure; ensure everything is **keyboard-operable** with visible focus; provide **alt text** and form labels; add **ARIA** only when semantics fall short; meet **WCAG** contrast ratios. Accessibility overlaps heavily with good SEO and UX.

cards.english: What are the Core Web Vitals?
cards.word: LCP (loading), INP (interactivity), and CLS (visual stability)
cards.grammarNote: **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint) measures when the main content appears; **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint) measures responsiveness to input; **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures unexpected layout jumps. Google uses them as ranking signals, so they connect performance work to business outcomes.

cards.english: What is CORS and why does it exist?
cards.word: A browser mechanism that lets a server opt in to cross-origin requests
cards.grammarNote: The **same-origin policy** blocks a page from reading responses from another origin. **CORS** lets the server relax that by returning `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers. For unsafe methods the browser sends a **preflight** `OPTIONS` request first. CORS is enforced by the **browser**, not the server — it's not a server-side security boundary.

cards.english: What is the same-origin policy?
cards.word: Scripts can only access resources from the same scheme + host + port
cards.grammarNote: The **same-origin policy** is a core browser security boundary: JS on `https://a.com` can't read data from `https://b.com` (or a different port/scheme). It prevents a malicious site from reading your logged-in data on another site. CORS, `postMessage`, and JSONP are the controlled ways to cross it.

cards.english: What is a closure in JavaScript?
cards.word: A function that retains access to variables from its defining scope
cards.grammarNote: A **closure** captures variables from the lexical scope where it was created, even after that scope has returned. It powers private state (module pattern, counters), callbacks, and currying. The classic gotcha is capturing a loop variable declared with `var` — use `let` for per-iteration binding.

cards.english: What is hoisting, and how do var, let, and const differ?
cards.word: Declarations are processed first; var is function-scoped, let/const are block-scoped
cards.grammarNote: **Hoisting** moves declarations to the top of their scope. `var` is function-scoped and initialized to `undefined` (accessible before assignment). `let`/`const` are block-scoped and in a **temporal dead zone** until declared (accessing them throws). `const` also forbids reassignment (but not mutation of objects).

cards.english: How is `this` determined in JavaScript?
cards.word: By how a function is called, not where it's defined (except arrow functions)
cards.grammarNote: `this` depends on the **call site**: the object before the dot for method calls, the global/undefined for plain calls, the new instance with `new`, or whatever `call`/`apply`/`bind` set. **Arrow functions** are the exception — they capture `this` lexically from their enclosing scope, which is why they're handy in callbacks.

cards.english: What's the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
cards.word: === compares without type coercion; == coerces types first
cards.grammarNote: `===` (strict) requires same type and value. `==` (loose) performs **type coercion** with surprising rules (`0 == ''`, `null == undefined`, `[] == false` are all true). Best practice: always use `===` to avoid coercion bugs, reserving `== null` as a deliberate null/undefined check.

cards.english: How does prototypal inheritance work?
cards.word: Objects delegate property lookups up a prototype chain
cards.grammarNote: Every JS object has a hidden link to a **prototype**; a missing property is looked up along the **prototype chain** until found or null. `class` syntax is sugar over this — methods live on the prototype, shared by all instances. Understanding the chain explains method resolution and memory sharing.

cards.english: What is the virtual DOM and why is it used?
cards.word: An in-memory tree diffed against the real DOM to batch minimal updates
cards.grammarNote: Direct DOM mutation is slow and error-prone. Frameworks build a lightweight **virtual DOM**, compute a **diff** between renders (**reconciliation**), and apply only the necessary real-DOM changes. It trades some memory/CPU for a declarative model and fewer expensive reflows. Keys help the diff match list items.

cards.english: What are Web Workers and Service Workers?
cards.word: Web Workers run JS off the main thread; Service Workers are a network proxy for offline/caching
cards.grammarNote: A **Web Worker** runs CPU-heavy work on a background thread, communicating via messages, so the UI stays responsive (no shared DOM access). A **Service Worker** sits between the app and network, intercepting requests to enable **offline caching, PWAs, and push notifications**.

cards.english: What are code splitting, tree shaking, and bundling?
cards.word: Bundling combines modules; tree shaking drops dead code; splitting loads code on demand
cards.grammarNote: A **bundler** (Webpack/Vite/esbuild) merges modules into optimized files. **Tree shaking** removes unused exports (relies on ES modules' static structure). **Code splitting** breaks the bundle so routes/features load lazily, shrinking the initial download and improving first-load performance.

cards.english: What is lazy loading and where do you apply it?
cards.word: Deferring loading of resources until they're actually needed
cards.grammarNote: **Lazy loading** delays fetching off-screen images (`loading="lazy"`), below-the-fold components, or route bundles until needed — cutting initial payload and speeding first paint. Pair it with **placeholders/skeletons** to avoid layout shift and with prefetching for likely-next content.

cards.english: Explain the CSS box model and box-sizing.
cards.word: Every element is content + padding + border + margin; box-sizing changes what width includes
cards.grammarNote: The **box model** wraps content in padding, then border, then margin. By default `width` sizes only the **content**, so padding/border add to the rendered size. Setting **`box-sizing: border-box`** makes `width` include padding and border — far more intuitive for layouts, hence its common global reset.

cards.english: When do you use Flexbox vs CSS Grid?
cards.word: Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts; Grid for two-dimensional layouts
cards.grammarNote: **Flexbox** lays out items along a single axis (a row or a column) with flexible spacing — ideal for navbars, toolbars, and distributing items in a line. **CSS Grid** controls **rows and columns simultaneously** — ideal for page-level and card layouts. They compose well: Grid for the macro layout, Flexbox within cells.

cards.english: How does CSS specificity decide which rule wins?
cards.word: Inline > ID > class/attribute/pseudo-class > element, then source order
cards.grammarNote: When rules conflict, the browser scores **specificity**: inline styles beat IDs, which beat classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, which beat element selectors. Ties break by **source order** (later wins). `!important` overrides all (avoid it). Understanding this prevents 'why won't my style apply' frustration.

cards.english: What are the fundamentals of responsive design?
cards.word: Fluid layouts, media queries, and a mobile-first viewport
cards.grammarNote: Responsive design adapts to screen size using **relative units** (%, rem, fr), **media queries** for breakpoints, and the **viewport meta tag**. A **mobile-first** approach styles the smallest screen by default and layers enhancements upward with `min-width` queries — generally simpler and more performant.

cards.english: What is hydration in SSR frameworks?
cards.word: Attaching client-side JS/event handlers to server-rendered HTML
cards.grammarNote: SSR sends fully-rendered HTML for a fast first paint, but it's static until **hydration** runs the JS to attach event listeners and make it interactive. Large bundles cause a gap where the page looks ready but isn't clickable. **Partial/islands** and **streaming/server-component** approaches reduce this cost.

cards.english: What makes an API RESTful?
cards.word: Stateless, resource-oriented URLs, standard HTTP verbs, and a uniform interface
cards.grammarNote: **REST** models the domain as **resources** (nouns) addressed by URLs, manipulated with HTTP **verbs** (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), and communicated **statelessly** — each request carries all context. Constraints also include cacheability and a uniform interface. It's a style, not a protocol.

cards.english: Which HTTP methods are idempotent and why does it matter?
cards.word: GET, PUT, DELETE (and HEAD) are idempotent; POST is not
cards.grammarNote: **Idempotent** means repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once — crucial for safe retries over unreliable networks. `PUT` (full replace) and `DELETE` qualify; `POST` (create) doesn't, since retrying can create duplicates. Use an **idempotency key** to make POST safely retryable.

cards.english: What do the main HTTP status code classes mean?
cards.word: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
cards.grammarNote: Know the common ones: **200/201/204** success, **301/302** redirects, **400** bad request, **401** unauthenticated, **403** forbidden, **404** not found, **409** conflict, **429** rate-limited, **500** server error, **503** unavailable. Using the right code lets clients react correctly.

cards.english: When would you use GraphQL instead of REST?
cards.word: GraphQL when clients need flexible, precise field selection and to avoid over/under-fetching
cards.grammarNote: **GraphQL** exposes one endpoint where clients request exactly the fields they need — solving REST's **over-fetching** (too much data) and **under-fetching** (N calls to assemble a view). Costs: complex caching (no HTTP cache per URL), query-cost/depth limits, and server complexity. REST stays simpler for CRUD.

cards.english: When is gRPC a good fit?
cards.word: High-performance internal service-to-service calls with strict contracts
cards.grammarNote: **gRPC** uses HTTP/2 and **Protobuf** binary serialization for low latency, streaming, and strongly-typed contracts via `.proto` files — ideal for internal microservice communication. It's less browser-friendly than REST/JSON, so it's usually kept east-west (service-to-service) rather than public-facing.

cards.english: How do you version an API?
cards.word: URL path (/v1/), headers, or query params — and avoid breaking changes
cards.grammarNote: Versioning lets you evolve without breaking clients. **URL versioning** (`/v1/users`) is explicit and cache-friendly; **header versioning** keeps URLs clean. Prefer **additive, non-breaking** changes so you rarely need a new version; when you must break, deprecate the old version on a clear timeline.

cards.english: Compare offset and cursor pagination.
cards.word: Offset is simple but drifts and slows on deep pages; cursor is stable and scales
cards.grammarNote: **Offset/limit** (`?page=5`) is easy but degrades on deep pages (the DB still scans skipped rows) and can skip/duplicate items if data changes. **Cursor (keyset)** pagination uses a pointer like `after=<last_id>`, giving stable, index-friendly results for large or live datasets.

cards.english: How do you implement API rate limiting?
cards.word: Token bucket or sliding window per client, returning 429 when exceeded
cards.grammarNote: Protects the service from abuse and overload. **Token bucket** refills tokens at a fixed rate and allows bursts up to capacity; **sliding window** smooths counts over time. Track counters in a shared store (Redis) keyed by API key/IP, return **429** with a `Retry-After` header.

cards.english: What makes a good API error response?
cards.word: Correct status code, a stable machine-readable error code, and a human-readable message
cards.grammarNote: Clients need to react programmatically, so return the right **HTTP status**, a stable **error code** (e.g. `"INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS"`), a clear **message**, and often a field for validation details and a correlation/trace ID. Consistency across endpoints (e.g. RFC 7807 problem+json) makes clients easier to build.

cards.english: What is HATEOAS?
cards.word: Responses include links to related actions, making the API self-describing
cards.grammarNote: **Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State** is REST's highest maturity level: a response embeds **links** telling the client what it can do next (e.g. an order with `cancel`/`pay` links). It decouples clients from hardcoded URLs but adds complexity, so it's often only partially adopted.

cards.english: What's the difference between PUT and PATCH?
cards.word: PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH applies a partial update
cards.grammarNote: **PUT** is a full replacement — you send the complete representation, and it's **idempotent**. **PATCH** modifies only the supplied fields, so it's smaller but not necessarily idempotent (depends on the operation). Use PUT to overwrite, PATCH to tweak specific fields.

cards.english: What are webhooks and when do you use them?
cards.word: Server-to-server callbacks that push events instead of the client polling
cards.grammarNote: A **webhook** is an HTTP callback: you register a URL, and the provider POSTs event data when something happens (payment succeeded, PR merged) — reversing the usual client-pull into a **push**. Consumers must handle **retries/duplicates** (idempotency) and **verify signatures** to trust the payload.

cards.english: What does an API gateway do?
cards.word: A single entry point handling routing, auth, rate limiting, and aggregation for backend services
cards.grammarNote: An **API gateway** fronts microservices, centralizing cross-cutting concerns: request **routing**, authentication, **rate limiting**, TLS termination, caching, and sometimes response aggregation. It simplifies clients (one endpoint) but is a potential bottleneck/SPOF, so it must be highly available.

cards.english: What is content negotiation?
cards.word: The client and server agree on response format/language via Accept headers
cards.grammarNote: Using headers like **`Accept: application/json`**, `Accept-Language`, and `Accept-Encoding`, the client states its preferences and the server responds with the best match (setting `Content-Type`, `Content-Language`). It lets one endpoint serve multiple representations (JSON/XML, gzip/brotli, locales).

cards.english: How should collection endpoints handle filtering, sorting, and field selection?
cards.word: Via query parameters — e.g. ?status=active&sort=-createdAt&fields=id,name
cards.grammarNote: Keep list endpoints flexible with **query params**: `?filter/status=`, `?sort=` (a `-` prefix for descending), and **sparse fieldsets** (`?fields=`) to reduce payload. This avoids proliferating custom endpoints. Validate and whitelist params to prevent abuse and expensive unindexed queries.

cards.english: How do ETags and conditional requests improve APIs?
cards.word: They enable caching (304s) and optimistic concurrency (avoid lost updates)
cards.grammarNote: The server returns an **ETag** (a version fingerprint). Clients send `If-None-Match` for cheap **revalidation** (304 Not Modified) and `If-Match` on writes so an update fails with **412** if the resource changed since they read it — preventing lost updates from concurrent edits.

cards.english: What is OpenAPI/Swagger and why use it?
cards.word: A machine-readable spec describing your API's endpoints, schemas, and auth
cards.grammarNote: **OpenAPI** (formerly Swagger) documents an API in a standard format that generates interactive docs, **client SDKs**, server stubs, and request validation/mocks. A spec-first workflow keeps docs and implementation in sync and gives consumers a reliable contract.

cards.english: What changes to an API are backward-compatible vs breaking?
cards.word: Adding optional fields/endpoints is safe; removing/renaming or changing types breaks clients
cards.grammarNote: **Non-breaking (additive)**: new optional request fields, new response fields, new endpoints. **Breaking**: removing/renaming fields, making an optional field required, changing a type or the meaning of a value, or tightening validation. Prefer additive evolution and treat responses as extensible so clients ignore unknown fields.

cards.english: How does an idempotency key make POST requests safe to retry?
cards.word: The server records the key and returns the original result on retries
cards.grammarNote: The client sends a unique **Idempotency-Key** header. The server stores the key with the outcome; a retry with the same key returns the **cached original response** instead of creating a duplicate (e.g. a double charge). Essential for payment/order APIs over unreliable networks.

cards.english: What is the Richardson Maturity Model?
cards.word: A 4-level scale of REST adoption from RPC-over-HTTP to full hypermedia
cards.grammarNote: **Level 0**: a single URI, HTTP as a tunnel (RPC). **Level 1**: separate **resources**. **Level 2**: proper **HTTP verbs and status codes** (where most 'RESTful' APIs sit). **Level 3**: **HATEOAS** hypermedia controls. It's a useful yardstick for how RESTful an API actually is.

cards.english: How do you design bulk/batch endpoints?
cards.word: Accept an array, process items, and return per-item statuses (often 207 Multi-Status)
cards.grammarNote: Batch endpoints reduce round-trips but complicate error handling: a request can **partially succeed**. Return a per-item result array (with individual status codes), consider **207 Multi-Status**, decide on all-or-nothing vs best-effort semantics, and cap batch size to bound resource use.

cards.english: Compare API keys, bearer tokens, and OAuth for API authentication.
cards.word: API keys identify an app; bearer/JWT authenticate requests; OAuth delegates user access
cards.grammarNote: **API keys** are simple app identifiers (coarse, easy to leak) good for server-to-server. **Bearer tokens/JWTs** carry authenticated identity per request. **OAuth 2.0** lets an app act on a **user's** behalf with scoped, revocable access. Always send credentials over TLS and scope them minimally.

cards.english: What's the difference between TCP and UDP?
cards.word: TCP is reliable, ordered, connection-oriented; UDP is fast, connectionless, best-effort
cards.grammarNote: **TCP** guarantees delivery and ordering via handshakes, acknowledgments, and retransmission — right for web, APIs, files. **UDP** just fires packets with no guarantees — right for real-time voice/video/gaming where a late packet is worse than a lost one. TCP trades latency for reliability.

cards.english: Explain the TCP three-way handshake.
cards.word: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK establishes a connection
cards.grammarNote: The client sends **SYN** (with an initial sequence number), the server replies **SYN-ACK** (acknowledging and sending its own), and the client sends **ACK**. Now both agree on sequence numbers and the connection is open. This round-trip cost is why connection reuse (keep-alive, pooling) matters.

cards.english: How does DNS resolution work?
cards.word: A recursive resolver walks root → TLD → authoritative servers to map a name to an IP
cards.grammarNote: The **recursive resolver** checks its cache, then queries a **root** server (points to `.com`), a **TLD** server (points to the domain's nameserver), and the **authoritative** server (returns the IP). Results are cached per their **TTL**. DNS is a distributed, hierarchical, heavily-cached system.

cards.english: What changed across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3?
cards.word: 1.1 = one request at a time per connection; 2 = multiplexing; 3 = QUIC over UDP
cards.grammarNote: **HTTP/1.1** suffers head-of-line blocking (one request per connection at a time). **HTTP/2** multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with header compression. **HTTP/3** runs over **QUIC (UDP)**, eliminating TCP-level head-of-line blocking and speeding up connection setup.

cards.english: How does HTTPS/TLS secure a connection?
cards.word: Asymmetric keys negotiate a shared symmetric key, then encrypt with it
cards.grammarNote: During the **TLS handshake**, the server presents a **certificate** (proving identity via a CA chain). Asymmetric crypto is used to agree on a shared **symmetric** session key, which then encrypts the actual data (symmetric is far faster). This gives confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.

cards.english: What are the key layers of the OSI/TCP-IP model?
cards.word: Link, Internet (IP), Transport (TCP/UDP), Application (HTTP)
cards.grammarNote: Layering separates concerns: **IP** handles addressing and routing between hosts; **TCP/UDP** handle host-to-process delivery (ports); the **application** layer (HTTP, DNS) is what apps speak. Each layer wraps the one above in its own header — **encapsulation**.

cards.english: What does a load balancer do, and L4 vs L7?
cards.word: Distributes traffic across servers; L4 routes by IP/port, L7 by request content
cards.grammarNote: A load balancer spreads requests to avoid overloading any one server and enables failover. **L4** balances at the transport layer (fast, opaque to content). **L7** understands HTTP, so it can route by path/host, terminate TLS, and do sticky sessions — more flexible, slightly more overhead.

cards.english: What is a CDN and how does it help?
cards.word: A geographically distributed cache that serves content from an edge near the user
cards.grammarNote: A **CDN** caches static (and increasingly dynamic) content at **edge** locations worldwide, cutting latency by serving from the nearest node and offloading the origin. It also absorbs traffic spikes and helps mitigate DDoS. Cache invalidation and TTLs are the main operational concerns.

cards.english: When would you use WebSockets over HTTP polling?
cards.word: For low-latency, bidirectional, real-time communication
cards.grammarNote: HTTP is request/response; for live updates you'd otherwise **poll** (wasteful) or **long-poll**. **WebSockets** upgrade a single connection to a persistent, full-duplex channel — ideal for chat, live dashboards, and games. For server→client-only streams, **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** are simpler.

cards.english: What's the difference between public and private IPs, and what is NAT?
cards.word: Private IPs are internal-only; NAT maps them to a shared public IP
cards.grammarNote: **Private** ranges (e.g. `10.0.0.0/8`, `192.168.0.0/16`) aren't routable on the internet. **NAT** (Network Address Translation) lets many private hosts share one **public** IP by rewriting addresses/ports — conserving scarce IPv4 addresses and adding a layer of isolation.

cards.english: What are the seven OSI layers?
cards.word: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
cards.grammarNote: Bottom-up: **Physical** (bits/cables), **Data Link** (frames/MAC), **Network** (IP/routing), **Transport** (TCP/UDP/ports), **Session**, **Presentation** (encryption/encoding), **Application** (HTTP/DNS). The practical **TCP/IP model** collapses these into 4 layers, but interviewers still ask the OSI names.

cards.english: What does ARP do?
cards.word: Resolves an IP address to a MAC address on the local network
cards.grammarNote: To deliver a packet on a LAN, a host needs the destination's **hardware (MAC) address**. **ARP** broadcasts 'who has this IP?' and caches the reply. It operates between the network and data-link layers. **ARP spoofing** — forging replies — enables man-in-the-middle attacks.

cards.english: What is ICMP, and how do ping and traceroute use it?
cards.word: A control/diagnostic protocol; ping tests reachability, traceroute maps the path
cards.grammarNote: **ICMP** carries control and error messages (not application data). **Ping** sends ICMP echo requests to measure reachability and round-trip time. **Traceroute** sends packets with increasing **TTL**, eliciting 'time exceeded' from each hop to reveal the route. Some networks block ICMP, limiting these tools.

cards.english: What is CIDR / subnetting?
cards.word: Splitting IP address space using a prefix length like /24 to define networks
cards.grammarNote: **CIDR** notation (`10.0.1.0/24`) uses a prefix length to mark how many leading bits are the **network** portion; the rest addresses hosts. A `/24` gives 256 addresses (254 usable). Subnetting segments networks for routing, isolation, and efficient address allocation — core to VPC/cloud networking.

cards.english: What are ports and some well-known ones?
cards.word: 16-bit numbers identifying a service on a host — 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH, 53 DNS
cards.grammarNote: A **port** lets one IP host many services; the OS routes a packet to the process bound to that port. Well-known: **80** HTTP, **443** HTTPS, **22** SSH, **53** DNS, **25/587** SMTP, **5432** Postgres, **6379** Redis. An `IP:port` pair plus protocol identifies a connection endpoint.

cards.english: What's the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
cards.word: A forward proxy fronts clients; a reverse proxy fronts servers
cards.grammarNote: A **forward proxy** sits in front of clients, sending requests on their behalf (corporate filtering, anonymity, caching). A **reverse proxy** (Nginx, a load balancer) sits in front of servers, terminating TLS, load balancing, caching, and hiding the backend — the pattern behind most web deployments and CDNs.

cards.english: How does TCP handle flow control and congestion control?
cards.word: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network
cards.grammarNote: **Flow control** uses the receiver's advertised **window** so a fast sender doesn't overwhelm a slow receiver. **Congestion control** (slow start, congestion avoidance, AIMD) probes network capacity and backs off on packet loss — preventing collapse. Together they make TCP adapt its send rate dynamically.

cards.english: What is HTTP keep-alive / connection reuse?
cards.word: Reusing one TCP connection for multiple requests instead of reopening each time
cards.grammarNote: Each new TCP+TLS connection costs round-trips. **Keep-alive** (persistent connections, default in HTTP/1.1) reuses a connection for many requests, cutting latency and load. **Connection pooling** applies the same idea for clients/databases. HTTP/2 goes further with multiplexing over one connection.

cards.english: What's the difference between latency, bandwidth, and throughput?
cards.word: Latency is delay per trip; bandwidth is max capacity; throughput is actual achieved rate
cards.grammarNote: **Latency** is how long one packet takes (dominated by distance/round-trips). **Bandwidth** is the pipe's theoretical max. **Throughput** is what you actually get, limited by latency, congestion, and protocol overhead. High bandwidth doesn't fix high latency — which is why CDNs move data closer to users.

cards.english: How does certificate trust (the chain of trust) work?
cards.word: Browsers trust root CAs, which sign intermediates, which sign your server certificate
cards.grammarNote: Your certificate is signed by an **intermediate CA**, itself signed by a **root CA** whose public key ships in the OS/browser trust store. The client verifies this **chain** up to a trusted root and checks the domain, expiry, and revocation. A missing intermediate is a common 'works in browser, fails in tooling' bug.

cards.english: What is mutual TLS (mTLS)?
cards.word: Both client and server present certificates to authenticate each other
cards.grammarNote: Standard TLS authenticates only the server. **mTLS** adds a **client certificate**, so the server also verifies the caller's identity — widely used for **service-to-service** auth in zero-trust architectures and service meshes, replacing shared secrets with cryptographic identity.

cards.english: What's the difference between IPv4 and IPv6?
cards.word: IPv4 is 32-bit (~4 billion addresses); IPv6 is 128-bit (effectively unlimited)
cards.grammarNote: **IPv4** exhausted its 32-bit address space, which is why **NAT** proliferated. **IPv6** uses 128-bit addresses (written in hex groups), removing the need for NAT, simplifying headers, and building in autoconfiguration. Adoption is gradual, so dual-stack and translation mechanisms bridge the two.

cards.english: What does a firewall do?
cards.word: Filters traffic against rules based on IP, port, protocol, or application data
cards.grammarNote: A **firewall** enforces a security policy on network traffic. **Stateless** filters judge each packet by header rules; **stateful** firewalls track connection state (allowing return traffic); **application/WAF** layers inspect HTTP payloads to block attacks like injection. Security groups in cloud VPCs are essentially distributed firewalls.

cards.english: What are sticky sessions, and what's the downside?
cards.word: Routing a user's requests to the same server; it breaks even load balancing and failover
cards.grammarNote: **Session affinity (sticky sessions)** pins a client to one backend so in-memory session state is found there. But it **uneven-loads** servers, loses the session if that server dies, and hampers scaling. The better pattern is **stateless** servers with session state in a shared store (Redis) or a signed token.

cards.english: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
cards.word: Authentication = who you are; authorization = what you're allowed to do
cards.grammarNote: **Authentication (AuthN)** verifies identity (password, token, biometric). **Authorization (AuthZ)** decides permitted actions on resources (roles, policies). You authenticate first, then authorize each request. Confusing the two leads to serious access-control bugs.

cards.english: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
cards.word: Untrusted input altering a query; prevent with parameterized queries
cards.grammarNote: Injection happens when user input is concatenated into SQL, letting an attacker change its logic (`' OR 1=1 --`). Prevent it with **parameterized queries / prepared statements** (the DB treats input as data, never code), plus least-privilege DB accounts and input validation. Never build SQL by string concatenation.

cards.english: What is XSS and how do you defend against it?
cards.word: Injecting malicious scripts into pages; defend with output encoding and CSP
cards.grammarNote: **Cross-Site Scripting** runs attacker JS in a victim's browser (stored, reflected, or DOM-based), stealing cookies or acting as the user. Defenses: **contextual output encoding/escaping**, treating input as data, `HttpOnly` cookies, and a **Content Security Policy** restricting script sources.

cards.english: What is CSRF and how do you prevent it?
cards.word: Tricking a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request; prevent with CSRF tokens / SameSite
cards.grammarNote: **Cross-Site Request Forgery** abuses the browser auto-sending cookies: a malicious site triggers a state-changing request to a site you're logged into. Defenses: unpredictable **CSRF tokens** tied to the session, **SameSite** cookies, and checking `Origin`/`Referer`. It targets cookie-based auth specifically.

cards.english: What's the difference between hashing and encryption?
cards.word: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is a one-way fingerprint
cards.grammarNote: **Encryption** transforms data so it can be **decrypted** with a key (for data you must read back). **Hashing** is **one-way** — you can't recover the input — used for integrity checks and password storage. Confusing them (e.g. 'encrypting' passwords) is a red flag in interviews.

cards.english: How should you store passwords?
cards.word: Salted, slow one-way hashes like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2
cards.grammarNote: Never store plaintext or fast hashes (MD5/SHA-256) of passwords. Use a **slow, adaptive** algorithm (**bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2**) with a per-user **salt** to defeat rainbow tables and make brute force expensive. A **pepper** (secret app-wide value) can add another layer.

cards.english: Compare JWTs and server-side sessions.
cards.word: Sessions store state on the server; JWTs are self-contained and stateless
cards.grammarNote: **Sessions** keep state server-side (or in a shared store) and hand the client an opaque ID — easy to revoke, needs lookup. **JWTs** carry signed claims so any server can validate without a lookup (great for scale/microservices), but are **hard to revoke** before expiry — mitigate with short TTLs + refresh tokens.

cards.english: What problem do OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect solve?
cards.word: OAuth delegates authorization; OIDC adds authentication (login) on top
cards.grammarNote: **OAuth 2.0** lets an app get **delegated access** to resources (e.g. 'access my Google Drive') without sharing a password, via access tokens and scopes. **OIDC** layers **identity** on OAuth, adding an **ID token** so you can use it for 'Log in with Google'. OAuth ≠ authentication by itself.

cards.english: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.word: Grant every user/service only the minimum access it needs
cards.grammarNote: Limiting permissions shrinks the **blast radius** of a compromise or bug. Apply it to DB accounts, API keys, IAM roles, and service-to-service calls. Related ideas: **defense in depth** (layered controls) and **zero trust** (verify every request, trust no network position).

cards.english: What is the OWASP Top 10?
cards.word: A ranked list of the most critical web application security risks
cards.grammarNote: The **OWASP Top 10** is the industry reference for common vulnerabilities — including **broken access control**, injection, cryptographic failures, security misconfiguration, and vulnerable dependencies. Citing it signals you think about security systematically rather than ad hoc.

cards.english: What is a Content Security Policy (CSP)?
cards.word: A header restricting which sources of scripts/styles/resources a page may load
cards.grammarNote: **CSP** is a defense-in-depth layer against **XSS**: the server sends a policy (e.g. `script-src 'self'`) and the browser refuses to execute inline scripts or load resources from disallowed origins. It won't fix an injection flaw alone but drastically limits what injected code can do.

cards.english: What is clickjacking and how do you prevent it?
cards.word: Tricking users into clicking a hidden framed page; prevent with X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors
cards.grammarNote: **Clickjacking** overlays your site in a transparent iframe over decoy content so victims click real buttons unknowingly. Defend by forbidding framing: **`X-Frame-Options: DENY`** or the CSP **`frame-ancestors`** directive, so your pages can't be embedded by other origins.

cards.english: What is SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)?
cards.word: Tricking the server into making requests to internal/unintended targets
cards.grammarNote: In **SSRF**, an attacker supplies a URL the server fetches (webhook, image loader), pointing it at **internal** services or cloud **metadata endpoints** (e.g. `169.254.169.254`) to steal credentials. Defend with strict allowlists, blocking internal IP ranges, and disabling unneeded redirects/protocols.

cards.english: What is command injection and how do you prevent it?
cards.word: Injecting OS commands via unsanitized input; avoid shells, use safe APIs with argument arrays
cards.grammarNote: When user input is concatenated into a **shell command**, an attacker can chain commands (`; rm -rf`). Prevent it by avoiding shell invocation entirely — call programs with an **argument array** (no shell parsing), validate/allowlist inputs, and never pass untrusted data to `eval`/`system`.

cards.english: What is a path traversal attack?
cards.word: Using ../ sequences to access files outside the intended directory
cards.grammarNote: If a filename comes from user input, `../../etc/passwd` can escape the intended folder. Defend by **canonicalizing** the resolved path and verifying it stays within the allowed base directory, rejecting `..`, and preferring opaque IDs mapped server-side to real paths rather than raw filenames.

cards.english: Why is insecure deserialization dangerous?
cards.word: Deserializing untrusted data can execute attacker-controlled code
cards.grammarNote: Native deserialization (Java, Python **pickle**, PHP) can instantiate arbitrary objects and trigger **gadget chains** leading to remote code execution. Never deserialize untrusted input with these formats — use **data-only** formats like JSON with strict schemas, and validate before constructing objects.

cards.english: What's the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
cards.word: Symmetric uses one shared key; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair
cards.grammarNote: **Symmetric** (AES) uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt — fast, but the key must be shared securely. **Asymmetric** (RSA, ECC) uses a **public key** to encrypt / verify and a **private key** to decrypt / sign — solving key distribution. In practice they combine: asymmetric to exchange a symmetric session key (as in TLS).

cards.english: How do digital signatures work?
cards.word: Sign a hash with a private key; anyone verifies it with the public key
cards.grammarNote: The signer hashes the message and **encrypts the hash with their private key**. Verifiers decrypt it with the **public key** and compare to their own hash of the message. This proves **integrity** (unchanged) and **authenticity** (only the private-key holder could sign) — the basis of certificates and JWT signing.

cards.english: What is multi-factor authentication?
cards.word: Requiring two or more independent factors: something you know, have, or are
cards.grammarNote: **MFA** combines factors from different categories — **knowledge** (password), **possession** (phone/TOTP/hardware key), **inherence** (biometric) — so a stolen password alone isn't enough. **TOTP** apps and **FIDO2/WebAuthn** hardware keys are far more phishing-resistant than SMS codes.

cards.english: How do you defend against brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks?
cards.word: Rate limiting, account lockout/backoff, CAPTCHA, and MFA
cards.grammarNote: Attackers automate password guessing (**brute force**) or replay leaked credentials (**credential stuffing**). Defenses: **rate limiting** and exponential **backoff** per account/IP, temporary lockouts, CAPTCHA on suspicion, breached-password checks, and MFA. Slow password hashing (bcrypt) also raises the cost.

cards.english: What are secure session management practices?
cards.word: Rotate IDs on login, set HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite, and expire/invalidate properly
cards.grammarNote: Protect session tokens: **regenerate the session ID on login** (prevents session fixation), store it in an **HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite** cookie (blocks XSS theft and CSRF), enforce idle and absolute **timeouts**, and invalidate server-side on logout. Never put session IDs in URLs (they leak via logs/referrers).

cards.english: How should applications manage secrets?
cards.word: Keep them out of code — use a secrets manager, env injection, and rotation
cards.grammarNote: Never hardcode API keys/passwords in source or commit them. Use a **secrets manager** (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) or injected environment variables, restrict access by least privilege, **rotate** regularly, and audit usage. Leaked secrets in git history are a top real-world breach cause — scan for them.

cards.english: What's the difference between encryption at rest and in transit?
cards.word: At rest protects stored data; in transit protects data moving over the network
cards.grammarNote: **In transit**: TLS encrypts data on the wire against eavesdropping/MITM. **At rest**: disk/database/field-level encryption protects data if storage is stolen or improperly accessed. Both are needed — plus care for data **in use**. Sensitive **PII** may also have regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA).

cards.english: What is defense in depth?
cards.word: Layering multiple independent controls so no single failure is catastrophic
cards.grammarNote: **Defense in depth** assumes any one control can fail, so it stacks them: network firewalls, WAF, input validation, least privilege, encryption, monitoring. An attacker must defeat every layer. It pairs with **zero trust** (verify every request, trust no implicit network position) for a resilient posture.

cards.english: What is threat modeling?
cards.word: Systematically identifying assets, threats, and mitigations early in design
cards.grammarNote: **Threat modeling** asks what you're protecting, who might attack, how, and what you'll do about it — often via frameworks like **STRIDE** (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation). Doing it at design time catches whole classes of flaws far cheaper than fixing them in production.

cards.english: How would you design a distributed rate limiter?
cards.word: Token bucket or sliding-window counter in a shared store (e.g. Redis)
cards.grammarNote: Token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket size and refills at a fixed rate; sliding window is smoother. It must be atomic and shared (Redis INCR + a Lua script) so limits hold across all servers. Reject over-limit requests with HTTP 429 and a Retry-After header.

cards.english: How do you approach capacity estimation in a design interview?
cards.word: Back-of-envelope: QPS, storage/day, bandwidth — then derive server & DB counts
cards.grammarNote: For example: DAU × actions × a peak factor → QPS; bytes/record × records/day → storage growth. Grounding the design in real numbers surfaces the true bottleneck (hot path, storage, or network) early and justifies your component choices.

cards.english: How do you approach a system design interview?
cards.word: Clarify requirements → estimate scale → sketch high-level design → deep-dive → address bottlenecks
cards.grammarNote: A structured flow beats jumping to components: **(1)** clarify functional & non-functional requirements and scope, **(2)** do rough **capacity estimation**, **(3)** define the API and data model, **(4)** draw a high-level architecture, **(5)** deep-dive one or two components, **(6)** identify bottlenecks, single points of failure, and tradeoffs. Drive the conversation and state assumptions.

cards.english: What's the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?
cards.word: Functional = what it does; non-functional = how well (scale, latency, availability)
cards.grammarNote: **Functional** requirements are features ('users can post and follow'). **Non-functional** requirements are the qualities that shape the architecture — expected **scale/QPS**, **latency** targets, **availability**, consistency needs, durability, and cost. The non-functional numbers are what actually drive your design choices.

cards.english: What do 'nines' of availability mean, and what are SLA/SLO/SLI?
cards.word: Nines quantify uptime; SLI measures, SLO targets, SLA promises (with penalties)
cards.grammarNote: **99.9%** ('three nines') allows ~8.7h downtime/year; **99.99%** ~52min. An **SLI** is the measured metric (e.g. success rate), an **SLO** is your internal target, and an **SLA** is the contractual promise to customers with penalties. Each extra nine costs disproportionately more redundancy.

cards.english: How do you eliminate single points of failure?
cards.word: Add redundancy: replicate components and remove any node whose loss takes down the system
cards.grammarNote: A **SPOF** is any component whose failure halts the whole system (a lone database, a single load balancer). Eliminate them with **redundancy** — multiple instances behind load balancers, replicated databases with failover, multi-AZ deployment. Ask 'what happens if this box dies?' for every box in your diagram.

cards.english: What's the difference between fault tolerance and graceful degradation?
cards.word: Fault tolerance masks failures; graceful degradation reduces functionality instead of failing entirely
cards.grammarNote: **Fault tolerance** keeps the system fully working despite failures (via redundancy/failover). **Graceful degradation** accepts reduced service — e.g. serve stale cache when the DB is down, or hide recommendations if that service fails — rather than a total outage. Both prioritize availability over perfection.

cards.english: What is the circuit breaker pattern?
cards.word: Stop calling a failing dependency to let it recover and fail fast
cards.grammarNote: Like an electrical breaker, it **trips open** after a dependency's failures cross a threshold, so calls fail fast (returning a fallback) instead of piling up and exhausting threads. After a cooldown it goes **half-open** to test recovery. It prevents one slow service from cascading into a system-wide outage.

cards.english: What is the bulkhead pattern?
cards.word: Isolate resources into pools so one failure can't sink the whole system
cards.grammarNote: Named after ship compartments, the **bulkhead** pattern partitions resources (separate thread pools/connection pools per dependency or tenant) so that exhaustion in one doesn't starve the rest. Combined with circuit breakers and timeouts, it contains failures and preserves partial availability.

cards.english: How should retries be done safely?
cards.word: Exponential backoff with jitter, capped attempts, and only on idempotent operations
cards.grammarNote: Naive immediate retries amplify load and can cause a **retry storm**. Use **exponential backoff** (increasing delays) plus **jitter** (randomization) to avoid synchronized retries, cap the attempts, and only retry **idempotent** or idempotency-keyed operations to avoid duplicate side effects.

cards.english: What are common load-balancing algorithms?
cards.word: Round-robin, least-connections, weighted, and consistent-hash/IP-hash
cards.grammarNote: **Round-robin** cycles evenly; **least-connections** favors the least-busy server (good for uneven request costs); **weighted** accounts for heterogeneous capacity; **hash-based** (IP/key) routes a client/key consistently to the same server (useful for cache locality or sticky needs). Health checks remove unhealthy nodes.

cards.english: Why should application servers be stateless?
cards.word: Stateless servers can be scaled and replaced freely; state lives in shared stores
cards.grammarNote: If a server holds session/user state in memory, requests must stick to it and losing it loses data. **Stateless** servers put state in a shared store (DB, Redis) or a signed token, so any instance can handle any request. This enables trivial **horizontal scaling**, rolling deploys, and failover.

cards.english: What are the tradeoffs between a monolith and microservices?
cards.word: Monoliths are simpler to build; microservices scale teams and services independently at high operational cost
cards.grammarNote: A **monolith** is easier to develop, test, and deploy early on, but couples everything. **Microservices** allow independent scaling, deployment, and team ownership — at the cost of network calls, distributed-systems complexity, and operational overhead. Most systems should **start monolithic** and split when scaling/organizational pain justifies it.

cards.english: How do services find each other (service discovery)?
cards.word: A registry maps service names to healthy instances, client-side or server-side
cards.grammarNote: In dynamic environments instances come and go, so hardcoded addresses fail. A **service registry** (Consul, etcd, Kubernetes DNS) tracks healthy instances. **Client-side** discovery has the caller pick an instance; **server-side** routes through a load balancer/gateway. Health checks keep the registry accurate.

cards.english: What problem do consensus algorithms like Raft and Paxos solve?
cards.word: Getting distributed nodes to agree on a value despite failures
cards.grammarNote: **Consensus** lets a cluster agree on one consistent decision (who's leader, the order of a log) even with crashes and network delays. **Raft** is designed for understandability (leader election + log replication); **Paxos** is the classic. They underpin coordination services (ZooKeeper/etcd) and replicated state machines.

cards.english: When do you use blob/object storage instead of a database?
cards.word: For large unstructured files — images, video, backups — served via URLs/CDN
cards.grammarNote: Databases are wrong for big binary files. **Object storage** (S3, GCS) stores files cheaply and durably at scale, addressed by key, and integrates with CDNs. Store the **file in object storage and its metadata/URL in the database**. Clients often upload/download directly via **presigned URLs** to bypass your servers.

cards.english: What is a Bloom filter and where is it used in system design?
cards.word: A probabilistic set that says 'definitely not present' or 'possibly present'
cards.grammarNote: A **Bloom filter** is a compact bit array that tests membership with **no false negatives** but possible false positives. It cheaply avoids expensive lookups — e.g. 'is this key even in the DB/cache?' to prevent **cache penetration**, or checking if a username might be taken before a full query.

cards.english: What's the difference between fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read for a feed?
cards.word: Write pre-computes feeds into follower inboxes; read assembles the feed at query time
cards.grammarNote: **Fan-out-on-write (push)** inserts each post into every follower's feed at post time — fast reads, but expensive for celebrities with millions of followers ('thundering herd'). **Fan-out-on-read (pull)** builds the feed when requested — cheap writes, slower reads. Real systems use a **hybrid**: push for normal users, pull for celebrities.

cards.english: How do distributed systems detect node failures?
cards.word: Heartbeats and health checks with timeouts declare a node dead
cards.grammarNote: Nodes send periodic **heartbeats**; if a coordinator misses several, it marks the node dead and reroutes/failover. The tradeoff is the **timeout**: too short causes false positives (flapping) on transient slowness; too long delays recovery. Distinguishing 'slow' from 'dead' is fundamentally hard (hence the CAP tension).

cards.english: How would you design a URL shortener?
cards.word: Generate a short unique key, store key→URL, and redirect on lookup (read-heavy, cache it)
cards.grammarNote: Core: map a **short key** to a long URL. Generate keys via a counter+**base62** encoding or a hash (handle collisions). Store in a key-value DB, **cache** hot keys (extremely read-heavy), and return a **301/302 redirect**. Discussion points: custom aliases, analytics, key length vs capacity, and expiration.

cards.english: What are the key components of a chat system design?
cards.word: Persistent connections (WebSocket), a message store, presence, and fan-out delivery
cards.grammarNote: Clients hold **WebSocket** connections to gateway servers (tracked in a connection registry). Messages persist to a store and are delivered to online recipients, queued for offline ones. Challenges: **presence/typing** indicators, ordering, delivery/read receipts, group fan-out, and scaling millions of concurrent connections.

cards.english: How would you design an autocomplete/typeahead system?
cards.word: Serve prefix matches from a trie/prefix index, precomputed and heavily cached
cards.grammarNote: Latency is critical, so precompute top suggestions per prefix (a **trie** with cached top-k, or a search engine's edge n-grams) and serve from memory/CDN. Update rankings offline from query logs. Discussion: personalization, ranking by popularity, debouncing client requests, and typo tolerance.

cards.english: How does a read-heavy design differ from a write-heavy one?
cards.word: Read-heavy leans on caching/replicas; write-heavy needs sharding, queues, and write-optimized stores
cards.grammarNote: For **read-heavy** systems, add caching layers, read replicas, and CDNs. For **write-heavy** systems, scale writes with **sharding**, buffer bursts through **queues**, batch writes, and consider write-optimized stores (**LSM-tree** databases like Cassandra) over update-in-place B-trees. Identify the ratio early — it dictates the architecture.

cards.english: What is event-driven architecture and why use it?
cards.word: Services communicate via asynchronous events, decoupling producers from consumers
cards.grammarNote: Instead of services calling each other directly (synchronous, tightly coupled), producers **emit events** to a broker and consumers react independently. This gives **loose coupling**, independent scaling, resilience (consumers can be down temporarily), and easy addition of new consumers — at the cost of eventual consistency and harder debugging.

cards.english: What's the difference between pub/sub and a message queue?
cards.word: A queue delivers each message to one consumer; pub/sub broadcasts to all subscribers
cards.grammarNote: A **queue** (point-to-point) has competing consumers where each message is processed once — good for distributing work. **Pub/sub** (topic) fans a message out to **every** subscriber — good for notifying many interested parties. Systems like Kafka blend both via consumer groups on partitions.

cards.english: When would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ?
cards.word: Kafka for high-throughput event streaming and replay; RabbitMQ for flexible routing and task queues
cards.grammarNote: **Kafka** is a distributed **log**: it retains ordered events per partition, enables **replay**, and handles massive throughput — ideal for event streaming/analytics. **RabbitMQ** is a traditional **broker** with rich routing (exchanges, bindings), acks, and per-message delivery — ideal for task queues and complex routing.

cards.english: Explain at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery.
cards.word: At-most-once may drop; at-least-once may duplicate; exactly-once is hard and costly
cards.grammarNote: **At-most-once**: fire and forget, messages can be lost. **At-least-once**: retried until acked, so consumers must handle **duplicates** (make them idempotent). **Exactly-once** is the ideal but expensive/complex — usually approximated with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers or dedup keys.

cards.english: Why must event consumers be idempotent?
cards.word: Because at-least-once delivery means the same event may arrive more than once
cards.grammarNote: Since most brokers redeliver on failure, a consumer must produce the same result whether it processes an event once or five times. Achieve idempotency with **dedup keys / processed-event tables**, upserts instead of inserts, or naturally idempotent operations. Non-idempotent consumers cause double-charges and duplicate records.

cards.english: What is event sourcing?
cards.word: Storing state as an append-only log of events, not just the current snapshot
cards.grammarNote: Rather than overwriting rows, you persist every **state-changing event**; current state is derived by replaying them. Benefits: full **audit history**, time-travel, and rebuildable read models. Costs: complexity, schema/versioning of events, and needing **snapshots** so replays don't get slow.

cards.english: What is CQRS?
cards.word: Separating the write model (commands) from the read model (queries)
cards.grammarNote: **Command Query Responsibility Segregation** uses different models/stores for writes vs reads, so each is optimized independently and scaled separately. It pairs naturally with event sourcing (events update read models). It adds complexity and **eventual consistency** between write and read sides, so reserve it for genuinely demanding domains.

cards.english: How do you manage a transaction across microservices (saga pattern)?
cards.word: A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions for rollback
cards.grammarNote: You can't hold a distributed ACID transaction across services, so a **saga** chains local transactions; if a later step fails, earlier ones are undone with **compensating transactions** (e.g. refund a charge). Orchestration uses a central coordinator; **choreography** uses events. It trades atomicity for availability.

cards.english: What is a dead-letter queue?
cards.word: A holding queue for messages that repeatedly fail processing
cards.grammarNote: After a message exceeds its retry limit (poison message, bad data), the broker moves it to a **DLQ** instead of blocking the main queue forever. This isolates failures for later inspection/replay and keeps healthy messages flowing. Monitoring DLQ depth is a key operational signal.

cards.english: What is backpressure and how do you handle it?
cards.word: When producers outpace consumers; handle by buffering, throttling, or shedding load
cards.grammarNote: If events arrive faster than they can be processed, queues grow unbounded and memory/latency blow up. **Backpressure** signals producers to slow down. Strategies: **bounded buffers**, consumer autoscaling, **rate limiting** producers, or **load shedding** (dropping low-priority events) to protect the system.

cards.english: How is message ordering guaranteed (or not) in a broker?
cards.word: Usually only within a partition/key, not globally across the topic
cards.grammarNote: Global ordering across a distributed topic would kill parallelism. Kafka guarantees order only **within a partition**, so you route related events to the same partition via a **key** (e.g. user ID). Consumers that need order must process a key's events serially; unrelated keys process in parallel.

cards.english: How do Kafka partitions and consumer groups enable scaling?
cards.word: Partitions parallelize a topic; each partition is consumed by one member of a group
cards.grammarNote: A topic is split into **partitions** for parallelism and ordering. A **consumer group** divides partitions among its members — each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, so you scale throughput by adding consumers up to the partition count. Multiple groups each get the full stream (pub/sub).

cards.english: What are offsets and why does committing them matter?
cards.word: An offset marks a consumer's position; when you commit it determines delivery semantics
cards.grammarNote: Each message has an **offset** (position in the partition); the consumer tracks/commits how far it's processed. **Commit after processing** → at-least-once (a crash re-reads uncommitted messages). **Commit before** → at-most-once (risk losing them). Offset handling is the lever behind delivery guarantees.

cards.english: What is log compaction?
cards.word: Retaining only the latest value per key instead of every message
cards.grammarNote: Normally a log expires by time/size. **Compaction** keeps the **most recent message per key**, so the log becomes a snapshot of current state you can replay to rebuild a cache or table (like a changelog). It's how Kafka supports 'infinite' retention of current state without unbounded growth.

cards.english: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?
cards.word: It avoids the dual-write problem when updating a DB and publishing an event
cards.grammarNote: Writing to the database and separately publishing an event can't be atomic — a crash between them loses consistency (**dual-write problem**). The **outbox** writes the event into an outbox table **in the same transaction**; a separate relay (often via **CDC**) then reliably publishes it. Now the DB commit and the event are all-or-nothing.

cards.english: How do you evolve event schemas safely?
cards.word: Use a schema registry with backward/forward-compatible changes
cards.grammarNote: Since producers and consumers deploy independently, event schemas must evolve without breaking either. A **schema registry** (Avro/Protobuf) enforces compatibility: **backward-compatible** changes (add optional fields, never remove/rename required ones) let old consumers read new events and vice versa. Breaking changes require a new event version.

cards.english: What's the difference between an event, a command, and a message?
cards.word: An event states a fact that happened; a command requests an action; a message is the envelope
cards.grammarNote: An **event** ('OrderPlaced') is an immutable statement of something that occurred — publishers don't know or care who consumes it. A **command** ('PlaceOrder') directs a specific handler to do something. **Message** is the generic transport term for either. Events promote loose coupling; commands imply a known recipient.

cards.english: What's the difference between choreography and orchestration?
cards.word: Choreography: services react to events independently; orchestration: a central coordinator directs the flow
cards.grammarNote: In **choreography**, each service listens for events and emits its own — fully decoupled but the overall workflow is implicit and hard to trace. In **orchestration**, a central **orchestrator** explicitly invokes each step — easier to understand and monitor, but a coordination bottleneck. Sagas can use either style.

cards.english: What is event-carried state transfer?
cards.word: Events include the data consumers need, so they don't call back to the source
cards.grammarNote: Instead of emitting a thin 'OrderPlaced (id=5)' that forces consumers to call back for details, the event carries the **relevant state** (customer, items, total). Consumers keep local read-optimized copies, reducing coupling and synchronous calls — at the cost of larger events and some data duplication.

cards.english: What is the competing consumers pattern?
cards.word: Multiple consumers pull from the same queue to process messages in parallel
cards.grammarNote: To scale processing, several consumer instances read from **one queue**; each message goes to whichever is free, so throughput scales with consumers and load balances naturally. It requires **idempotent** handlers (redelivery) and gives up strict ordering across consumers — the standard way to scale a work queue.

cards.english: How should a consumer handle transient processing failures?
cards.word: Retry with exponential backoff, then route to a dead-letter queue after a limit
cards.grammarNote: Transient errors (a downstream blip) warrant **retries with exponential backoff + jitter** so you don't hammer a struggling dependency. Cap the attempts; a persistently failing (**poison**) message then goes to a **DLQ** for inspection instead of blocking the queue. Distinguish retryable from non-retryable errors.

cards.english: What's the difference between stream and batch processing?
cards.word: Batch processes bounded data periodically; streaming processes unbounded data continuously
cards.grammarNote: **Batch** (Spark, nightly jobs) runs over a fixed dataset on a schedule — high throughput, high latency. **Stream** processing (Flink, Kafka Streams) handles events continuously as they arrive — low latency, but must deal with **windowing**, out-of-order/late events, and watermarks. Choose by latency needs.

cards.english: How is 'exactly-once' processing achieved in practice?
cards.word: At-least-once delivery combined with idempotent consumers or transactional dedup
cards.grammarNote: True end-to-end exactly-once is expensive, so systems approximate it: deliver **at-least-once** and make effects **idempotent** (dedup by message ID/processed-log), or use framework transactions (Kafka's transactional producer + read-process-write) to atomically consume and produce. The practical goal is 'effectively once', not magic.

cards.english: What do the SOLID principles stand for?
cards.word: Single-responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion
cards.grammarNote: **S**: a class has one reason to change. **O**: open for extension, closed for modification. **L**: subtypes must be substitutable for their base. **I**: prefer small, focused interfaces. **D**: depend on abstractions, not concretions. Together they guide maintainable, loosely-coupled OO design.

cards.english: What are the four pillars of OOP?
cards.word: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism
cards.grammarNote: **Encapsulation** hides internal state behind an interface. **Abstraction** exposes only essential behavior. **Inheritance** shares behavior via an is-a hierarchy. **Polymorphism** lets one interface serve many types (e.g. overriding). Modern advice: favor **composition over inheritance** to avoid rigid hierarchies.

cards.english: Why favor composition over inheritance?
cards.word: Composition is more flexible and avoids brittle, deep class hierarchies
cards.grammarNote: Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent's implementation (the **fragile base class** problem) and forces an is-a relationship. **Composition** builds behavior by combining smaller objects (has-a), which you can swap at runtime — this underlies the Strategy pattern and dependency injection.

cards.english: What is the Singleton pattern and what's the criticism?
cards.word: Ensures one shared instance; criticized as hidden global state
cards.grammarNote: **Singleton** guarantees a single instance with global access (e.g. a config or connection pool). Criticisms: it's effectively a **global variable**, hurts testability (hard to mock/reset), and can hide dependencies. Often better replaced by **dependency injection** of a single-scoped instance.

cards.english: What problem does the Factory pattern solve?
cards.word: It encapsulates object creation so callers depend on an interface, not concrete classes
cards.grammarNote: A **factory** centralizes the logic of which concrete class to instantiate, so client code stays decoupled from specific types (supporting the Open/Closed and Dependency-Inversion principles). Add a new type by extending the factory, not editing every call site. Variants include Factory Method and Abstract Factory.

cards.english: Describe the Strategy pattern.
cards.word: Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface, chosen at runtime
cards.grammarNote: **Strategy** defines a family of algorithms (e.g. sort orders, pricing rules) as separate classes implementing one interface, letting you swap behavior at runtime without conditionals. It's composition in action and a clean alternative to sprawling `if/else` or `switch` blocks.

cards.english: Describe the Observer pattern.
cards.word: Subjects notify a list of subscribers automatically when their state changes
cards.grammarNote: **Observer** establishes a one-to-many dependency: when the **subject** changes, all registered **observers** are notified. It underpins event systems, UI data-binding, and reactive frameworks. It decouples the source from consumers but can make control flow harder to trace.

cards.english: Describe the Decorator pattern.
cards.word: Wrap an object to add behavior dynamically without changing its class
cards.grammarNote: **Decorator** wraps an object in another implementing the same interface, layering behavior (e.g. adding compression then encryption to a stream). It's a composition-based alternative to subclass explosion — you mix capabilities at runtime instead of a class per combination.

cards.english: Describe the Adapter pattern.
cards.word: Translate one interface into another so incompatible classes can work together
cards.grammarNote: An **adapter** wraps an existing class and exposes the interface a client expects — like a plug adapter. It's the go-to for integrating a **third-party or legacy** API without changing your code or theirs. Contrast with Facade (simplifies a subsystem) and Decorator (adds behavior).

cards.english: What is dependency injection and why is it useful?
cards.word: Supplying a class's dependencies from outside instead of creating them internally
cards.grammarNote: **DI** hands a class its collaborators (via constructor/setter) rather than having it `new` them, implementing the **Dependency Inversion** principle. Benefits: easy to swap implementations, **testable** (inject mocks), and clear dependencies. It's the backbone of frameworks like Spring and Angular.

cards.english: What are the three categories of the classic GoF design patterns?
cards.word: Creational, Structural, and Behavioral
cards.grammarNote: **Creational** patterns handle object creation (Factory, Builder, Singleton, Prototype, Abstract Factory). **Structural** patterns compose objects into larger structures (Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite). **Behavioral** patterns manage communication and responsibility (Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Iterator).

cards.english: What problem does the Builder pattern solve?
cards.word: Constructing complex objects step by step, avoiding telescoping constructors
cards.grammarNote: When an object has many optional parameters, constructors explode into confusing overloads (**telescoping constructors**). The **Builder** provides a fluent, readable step-by-step construction (`.name(x).age(y).build()`), can enforce required fields, and can produce **immutable** objects. Common for configuration and complex value objects.

cards.english: How does Abstract Factory differ from Factory Method?
cards.word: Factory Method creates one product; Abstract Factory creates families of related products
cards.grammarNote: **Factory Method** defines one overridable creation method for a single product type. **Abstract Factory** groups multiple factory methods to produce a **family** of compatible objects (e.g. a `WindowsUIFactory` making matching buttons, checkboxes, menus). Use it to keep a set of related products consistent.

cards.english: What is the Facade pattern?
cards.word: A simplified interface hiding the complexity of a subsystem
cards.grammarNote: A **Facade** provides one convenient entry point over a complicated subsystem of many classes, so clients don't wire the internals themselves. It reduces coupling to subsystem details. Unlike an Adapter (which converts an interface) or Decorator (which adds behavior), a Facade **simplifies**.

cards.english: What is the Proxy pattern and its common uses?
cards.word: A stand-in that controls access to another object
cards.grammarNote: A **Proxy** implements the same interface as a target and mediates access — for **lazy loading** (virtual proxy), **access control** (protection proxy), **caching**, or **remote** calls (a stub for a remote object). It shares Decorator's wrapping structure but its intent is controlling access, not adding features.

cards.english: What is the Command pattern?
cards.word: Encapsulate a request as an object, enabling queuing, logging, and undo
cards.grammarNote: The **Command** pattern turns an action + its parameters into an object with an `execute()` (and often `undo()`). This decouples the invoker from the receiver and enables **queuing, scheduling, logging, and undo/redo** — the basis of task queues, transactional operations, and editor undo stacks.

cards.english: What is the Template Method pattern?
cards.word: A base class defines an algorithm's skeleton, letting subclasses fill in specific steps
cards.grammarNote: The **Template Method** puts the invariant algorithm structure in a base-class method that calls overridable **hook steps**. Subclasses customize the steps without changing the overall flow (e.g. a data-processing pipeline where only parse/transform vary). It's the inheritance-based cousin of Strategy.

cards.english: What is the State pattern?
cards.word: Encapsulate state-specific behavior in objects, so the object changes behavior with its state
cards.grammarNote: The **State** pattern replaces sprawling `if/switch` on a status field with a **state object** per state, each implementing the same interface; transitions swap the current state object. It's ideal for state machines (order lifecycle, connection states) — adding a state means adding a class, not editing conditionals.

cards.english: What is the Chain of Responsibility pattern?
cards.word: Pass a request along a chain of handlers until one handles it
cards.grammarNote: Each handler either processes the request or forwards it to the next — decoupling sender from receiver and letting you add/reorder handlers freely. It's the model behind **middleware pipelines** (auth → logging → rate-limit → route) and event bubbling. Handlers stay small and single-purpose.

cards.english: What is the Iterator pattern?
cards.word: Provide sequential access to a collection's elements without exposing its structure
cards.grammarNote: An **Iterator** offers a uniform way to traverse a collection (`hasNext()`/`next()`) regardless of its internal representation (array, tree, list). It's so useful it's built into most languages (`for...of`, `Iterable`), enabling one loop to work over any conforming collection and even lazy/infinite sequences.

cards.english: What is the Repository pattern?
cards.word: An abstraction over data access that hides persistence behind a collection-like interface
cards.grammarNote: A **Repository** mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers, exposing methods like `findById`/`save` so business logic isn't coupled to SQL or a specific ORM/data source. Benefits: swappable storage, easier testing (mock the repo), and centralized query logic. Risk: leaking into a thin pass-through with little value.

cards.english: What do MVC and MVVM separate, and why?
cards.word: They split UI concerns: data (Model), presentation (View), and coordination (Controller/ViewModel)
cards.grammarNote: **MVC** separates the **Model** (data/logic), **View** (UI), and **Controller** (handles input, updates model). **MVVM** replaces the controller with a **ViewModel** that exposes bindable state, enabling two-way **data binding** (Angular, WPF). Both aim to decouple UI from logic for testability and maintainability.

cards.english: What do DRY, KISS, and YAGNI mean?
cards.word: Don't Repeat Yourself, Keep It Simple, You Aren't Gonna Need It
cards.grammarNote: **DRY**: eliminate duplicated knowledge (but avoid over-abstracting coincidental similarity). **KISS**: prefer the simplest solution that works. **YAGNI**: don't build for speculative future needs. Together they push toward simple, non-duplicated code that solves today's problem — a counterweight to over-engineering.

cards.english: What's the difference between coupling and cohesion?
cards.word: Coupling is interdependence between modules; cohesion is focus within a module
cards.grammarNote: Good design aims for **low coupling** (modules depend on each other minimally, via interfaces) and **high cohesion** (each module's parts serve one clear purpose). Tightly coupled, low-cohesion code is fragile and hard to change. Most patterns and SOLID principles ultimately serve these two goals.

cards.english: What's the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
cards.word: An interface is a pure contract; an abstract class can provide shared state and implementation
cards.grammarNote: An **interface** declares methods with no state (a capability contract); a class can implement **many**. An **abstract class** can hold fields and concrete methods to share among subclasses but allows only **single** inheritance. Rule of thumb: interface for 'can-do' capabilities, abstract class for a shared 'is-a' base with common code.

cards.english: What's the difference between method overloading and overriding?
cards.word: Overloading = same name, different parameters (compile-time); overriding = subclass redefines a method (runtime)
cards.grammarNote: **Overloading** defines multiple methods with the same name but different signatures, resolved at **compile time** (static polymorphism). **Overriding** replaces an inherited method's behavior in a subclass, resolved at **runtime** via dynamic dispatch — the mechanism behind polymorphism. Different concepts despite similar names.

cards.english: What are some common anti-patterns to avoid?
cards.word: God object, spaghetti code, magic numbers, premature optimization, copy-paste programming
